chapters.title: Hand Up the Credit So Your Wins Get Rewarded
chapters.hook: You just pulled off the win of the year, and you want to tell the whole meeting how you did it. Your boss is listening. How do you get rewarded for being brilliant without making them feel small?
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think great work speaks for itself and bosses will happily reward it. Actually, your win pays off when it makes your boss look good, because the people above you want to feel they still stand higher.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When you win something big, give part of the glory to your boss, so your success makes them shine.
chapters.tryThisNow: Write one line in your next status update today that names how your boss helped your latest win. You will see the update read as a team success, and your boss will notice.

memorableLines.text: Tell your wins so the person above you looks smart for backing you.

breakdown.fastRead:
Maya has just landed the biggest client the team has ever had, and she is ready to tell Monday's meeting how. The manager at the head of the table is smiling a little too tightly. Maya expects a raise, because at school good work got a good grade. But bosses have their own pride, so when you shine alone, they can look small next to you.

Galileo once had the same problem, and his was about money. He needed steady support, but the many patrons he gave his inventions to sent only gifts. Then he found four moons circling Jupiter, the Medici family's symbol, and he named the moons after them. Cosimo II de' Medici made him the family's official scientist, with a steady salary. The discovery paid off because it made his patrons look grand instead of making him look grander.

So Maya can still tell the story, but it can open with the push the manager gave. You can ease off if the boss is on the way out, because a boss losing power can no longer hold your brilliance against you. With most bosses, though, the move is simple. Share your big wins so they shine on the person above you, and the reward comes back to you.

Maya has just landed the biggest client the team has ever had. At Monday's meeting, she is ready to walk everyone through the win, step by step. The manager at the head of the table is smiling a little too tightly. Maya expects this story to earn a raise. But it is about to make the manager feel like the least useful person in the room.

Maya's hope feels reasonable because it is how school worked. You did good work, the teacher saw it, and you got the grade. Bosses are different, because they have their own pride. Your reward is decided by a person with feelings, not by the quality of the work alone. When you shine too brightly alone, they can look small standing next to you. A worker who keeps outshining the boss in meetings often finds the best projects quietly going elsewhere. Nobody says why, so the worker blames bad luck.

Each one sent a gift, and none of them took him on for good. Then he found four moons circling Jupiter. The facts of the win stay the same, and only the order of the story changes. Share your big wins so they shine on the person above you, and the reward comes back to you.
breakdown.fullRead:
Maya has just landed the biggest client the team has ever had. At Monday's meeting, she is ready to walk everyone through the win, step by step. The manager at the head of the table is smiling a little too tightly. Maya expects this story to earn a raise. But it is about to make the manager feel like the least useful person in the room. Nobody will say so out loud, and that silence is part of the trouble.

Maya's hope feels reasonable because it is how school worked. You did good work, the teacher saw it, and you got the grade. Bosses are different, because they have their own pride. Your reward is decided by a person with feelings, not by the quality of the work alone. When you shine too brightly alone, they can look small standing next to you. A worker who keeps outshining the boss in meetings often finds the best projects quietly going elsewhere. Nobody says why, so the worker blames bad luck.

The people above you want to feel they stand higher, and that holds even when they like you. Almost everyone carries some doubt about their own talent, and people in high places want to feel secure and superior. So a boss who is fond of you can still turn on you once you make them feel second best. You can even outshine a boss without trying, simply by being quick or charming in the room. Some bosses are more unsure of themselves than others, so you cannot assume yours is the calm kind. A favor from a boss is no free pass either, so never let it go to your head.

The sharpest warning is Nicolas Fouquet, who ran the money for King Louis XIV of France. Fouquet was rich and charming, but Fouquet was passed over for prime minister, sensed the king's favor slipping, and wanted to win it back. So Fouquet held the grandest party anyone had seen, at a splendid new home, with the king as guest of honor. There was a rich meal, new music, a new play, beautiful gardens, and fireworks, and the best minds of Europe came to enjoy it. Fouquet expected thanks, but the next morning the king's men arrested Fouquet.

Fouquet was tried for stealing from the country and was locked away in a far-off prison for the rest of Fouquet's life. The party had been meant as a gift, but every guest spent the night admiring the host. Louis was proud and wanted to be the center of every room, so the evening felt like an insult. The king then hired the same designers to build something even grander, the palace of Versailles. Fouquet thought showing taste and wealth would win the king over, but it only made the king feel smaller.

Galileo once had the same problem, and his was about money. He needed steady support for his research, but he gave his inventions to many different patrons. Each one sent a gift, and none of them took him on for good. Then he found four moons circling Jupiter. Jupiter was the Medici family's symbol, so he named the moons after them and offered the find as a sign of their greatness. Cosimo II de' Medici made him the family's official scientist, with a steady salary. The discovery paid off because it made his patrons look grand instead of making him look grander. Fouquet's brilliance pushed the king into the shade, but Galileo's brilliance lit up the family above him.

None of this means doing worse work, but be careful how much of your talent you display to those above you. Galileo's moons were real, and the find was still his own work. Stars can be as bright as the sun, but you never see them beside it in the sky. So you can be as strong as you are, as long as you find ways to make the person above you look stronger. If your idea is better, link it to something your boss already said. If you know more, ask for their advice now and then, so they get to feel like the teacher. The same goes for home, where a parent or an aunt who has long run things can feel pushed aside by your quick fix.

So Maya can still tell the story of the client, but in a different way. The story can open with the push the manager gave and the door the manager opened. The facts of the win stay the same, and only the order of the story changes. The manager now looks smart for backing her, so the manager has a reason to speak up for her next time. The team still learns who did the work, because she is the one telling the story.

Use your judgment, because this move has limits. You cannot worry about upsetting everyone, so save this care for the people who hold power over you. You can ease off if the boss is on the way out, because a boss losing power can no longer hold your brilliance against you. Even then, never rub it in, because outshining a very weak boss can look cruel. If your boss is firmly in place and you know you are more able, be patient, because power fades in time. With most bosses, though, the move is simple. Share your big wins so they shine on the person above you, and the reward comes back to you.

examples.title: The sales deal you closed alone
examples.scenario: Priya spent three months chasing a big client, and this morning the client finally signed. The team meeting starts in five minutes, and the manager will ask how the deal came together. She did most of the work, so it feels fair to tell the story as a solo win. She stands up, ready to speak, and has to choose what to say first.
examples.whatToDo: Open by thanking the manager for giving you the account and the room to chase it, then walk through how the deal came together.
examples.whyItMatters: The manager now looks smart for trusting her, so they will want to back her on the next big client.

examples.title: Your science fair project wins first place
examples.scenario: Marcus built a water filter for the science fair, and it just won first place. A local newspaper reporter is asking him a few questions near the stage. His teacher, who helped plan the project and stayed late twice, is standing a few feet away. He wants the article to be about one smart student and is about to answer.
examples.whatToDo: Mention the teacher by name in your first answer, and say the late sessions with them are where the idea really took shape.
examples.whyItMatters: A teacher who looks good in print will push him for the next contest and write a stronger reference letter.

examples.title: You saved the family reunion
examples.scenario: Leah's aunt has hosted the family reunion for ten years, but this year the rented hall fell through. Leah found a park pavilion, booked it, and sorted out the food in two days. Now the whole family group chat is asking who saved the day. Her thumbs are over the keyboard, and a message that starts with "I fixed it" is half typed.
examples.whatToDo: Post that you just followed the aunt's playbook, and ask the aunt to give the welcome toast like every year.
examples.whyItMatters: The aunt still feels like the host, so Leah gains a grateful ally instead of a hurt relative at the picnic.

questions.prompt: You led a new city park project, and it opens to big crowds. The mayor's office asks your department head for a statement. What do you do?
choices: Draft a statement for your department head, so the park becomes their win too.
Send the mayor's office your own statement, since you led the project day to day.
Stay out of it, so you don't look like you want the spotlight.
questions.explanation: Drafting the statement for your boss hands up the credit, so the park makes them shine too. Sending your own statement feels fair, but it follows the mistaken idea that great work gets rewarded without your boss.

questions.prompt: A baker's assistant invents a pastry that sells out daily. They tell regulars the owner's recipes were getting stale. The owner cuts their hours. What belief led them wrong?
choices: Believing the owner was too busy to notice what staff said to regulars.
Believing a hit pastry would make the owner happy and eager to give more hours.
Believing the pastry should be sold, rather than kept off the menu to protect the owner.
questions.explanation: The trap is expecting the boss to be glad about a win that makes them look small. Thinking the owner wouldn't notice misses it. The pastry was fine, but it needed to honor the owner's bakery.

questions.prompt: A front desk worker gets glowing guest reviews. They tell the hotel manager the reviews show the manager's training works. What most likely happens next?
choices: The manager just ignores the comment, because reviews only ever help the worker who earned them.
The manager distrusts the worker, since praise from staff always sounds fake to bosses.
The manager gives the worker better shifts, because the reviews make the manager look good.
questions.explanation: Tying the reviews to the manager's training lets the win make them shine, so they reward the worker. Thinking reviews only help the one who earned them follows the mistaken idea that great work rewards itself.

questions.prompt: A reporter friend says, "My big scoop is all over the internet, so my editor will be thrilled and give me the next big story." What is your best reply?
choices: Great, so tell other outlets you found the story with no help from anyone.
Then let the editor's name go on the story instead, so you stay out of view.
Explain how your editor's push shaped the story, so the scoop makes them look good.
questions.explanation: Crediting your editor's push gives them part of the glory, so the scoop makes them shine. Bragging to other outlets follows the mistaken idea that a big win pleases the boss on its own. Putting only their name on it goes too far.

questions.prompt: A designer names their winning app feature after their manager's favorite project. Soon the manager gives them a lead role. Why did this work?
choices: The win made the manager look good, so helping the designer also helped the manager.
The feature was so good that any manager would have rewarded the designer for it anyway.
The manager felt flattered by the name, so the feature's actual quality didn't matter.
questions.explanation: Your success should make your boss shine, and naming the feature after their project did that. Thinking any manager would reward great work misses that the win had to make the manager look good. The flattery only worked because the win was real.

questions.prompt: Your idea for a new staff schedule saved your clinic a lot of money. The clinic director will report the results to the board next week. What do you do?
choices: Ask to present it yourself, since the board should know whose idea it was.
Give the director a slide that ties the savings to their own goal.
Say nothing about the schedule, so nobody feels outdone by your idea.
questions.explanation: A slide tied to the director's goal lets the savings make them shine, so they have a reason to back you. Asking to present it yourself follows the mistaken idea that great work earns reward on its own. Saying nothing hides the win, so it can't help anyone.

questions.prompt: Your old manager has been moved aside and has no say over pay or projects now. A new leader runs the team, and you just won a big contract. What do you do?
choices: Share your part, and link the win to the new leader's goals.
Share your part, and trust the new leader to see its value on their own.
Give the old manager most of the credit, the same as you always do.
questions.explanation: A boss losing power can no longer hold your win against you, so you can own your part. The new leader is the one above you now, so tie the win to their goals. Trusting them to see its value alone follows the mistaken idea that great work gets rewarded by itself. Putting the old manager first follows the rule past its limit.

reviewCards.front: You're asked to give a short talk at the company party about the new app your team launched under your manager.
reviewCards.back: Open by thanking your manager's vision, then share your part, because a manager who shares the applause will want you on the next big project.

reviewCards.front: Your shop's sales doubled after your window display idea. Why would thanking the store manager in the staff meeting help your career?
reviewCards.back: Because the manager then looks like a smart leader for backing you, so they have a reason to reward you instead of feeling outdone.

reviewCards.front: When a grant you wrote gets approved and you announce it, the person to thank first is ...
reviewCards.back: ... the head of your group, because the win then adds to their name, and they become the one pushing for your next step.

reviewCards.front: A temp worker fixed a messy filing system in a week and expected a job offer, but the office head hired someone else.
reviewCards.back: They assumed good work gets rewarded by itself, but showing the office head how the fix made their office look better would have given them a reason to hire.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what does 'hand up the credit' mean, and why does it work?
reviewCards.back: When you win big, share the glory with your boss so your success makes them shine, because a boss who looks good rewards you.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Tie your wins to your boss's goals, so your good work makes them look good in front of others.

ifThenPlans.plan: When a coworker stops by my desk and says, "Nice job on that", I thank them and tell them which part came from my boss's idea or support.
When my boss's own manager asks me how the project went, I start my answer with what my boss set up, and only then share my part.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before you leave work today, open your last project update. Add one sentence that links the result to a goal your boss cares about, so they can pass it up the line.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each time you walk into your weekly check-in with your boss, bring one recent win. Show them how it helps their goals, so they can use it when they report to their own boss.

chapters.title: Why Your Best Friend May Be Your Worst Hire
chapters.hook: You need someone to handle a job that truly matters, and two names are in front of you: your closest friend and a skilled stranger. Why could the friend you trust most be the riskier choice?
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think a friend is the safest person to rely on, because a friend will never let them down. Actually, a friend can be the bigger risk, because warm feelings hide weak skills and unspoken envy.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When a job really matters, choose the person with the skill, and keep your friends for friendship.
chapters.tryThisNow: Write down today the one job you most need done well, then list the skills it takes before you think of any names. This keeps your liking for someone from choosing for you.

memorableLines.text: Pick your helper for what they can do, not how they make you feel.

breakdown.fastRead:
Who is the safer pick for a job that really matters: your closest friend, or a stranger who knows the work? Noor must decide this week, because her new restaurant needs someone to run the money. Callum, her best friend, has offered, and a skilled bookkeeper has applied too. He feels obvious, because a friend would never let you down. But friends often hide their faults to keep the peace.

Michael III, ruler of the Byzantine Empire, made that same choice. He needed someone he could trust at the top, so he turned to his best friend, Basilius. Basilius ran the royal stables and had no experience of government. Michael had already paid for his schooling, and now gave him wealth and high rank, but Basilius kept wanting more. In the end he had Michael killed and took the throne. Michael's warm feelings had hidden the danger.

The law itself is blunt. Be wary of friends, because envy makes them betray you and closeness spoils them. Hire a former enemy, who has more to prove, and if you have no enemies, find a way to make some. You can go easier than the law: keep your friends, and just stop handing them jobs they can't do. A friend may suit dirty work, or can take the blame when a plan fails, but making a friend the scapegoat costs you that friend for good. So Noor hires the bookkeeper and keeps Callum for Sunday dinners. The skilled stranger is the safer pick, because liking someone can stop you checking what they can do. Let the job pick the person, and let your friends stay friends.

breakdown.fullRead:
Who is the safer pick for a job that really matters: your closest friend, or a stranger who knows the work? Noor must decide this week, because her new restaurant needs someone to run the money. Callum, her best friend, has offered, and a skilled bookkeeper she hardly knows has applied too. One choice feels warm and the other feels cold. The answer turns on a question she hasn't asked yet, which is who can actually do the job.

Callum feels obvious, because a friend would never let you down. You know each other, you share jokes, and you have helped each other through hard times. But friends often hide their faults and agree with you to avoid a fight, so you may not know them as well as you think. Someone can be a wonderful friend and still be poor with money. Work needs skill and a little distance, and warm feelings can hide that. When the job goes badly, you also can't speak plainly, because the friendship is at stake.

The law behind this is blunt. It says to be wary of friends, because envy makes them quick to betray you and closeness makes them spoiled and bullying. A friend you hire may feel the weight of owing you, and people often come to resent what they owe. Closeness can also leave a friend spoiled and demanding. That is why the law says you have more to fear from friends than from enemies. It tells you to hire a former enemy instead, because that person has more to prove and will be more loyal. It even says that if you have no enemies, you should find a way to make some.

Michael III, ruler of the Byzantine Empire, shows how this can go. A young stable hand named Basilius saved him from a wild horse, and the two became best friends. Michael made him head of the royal stables, sent him to school, and kept him close. Then Michael needed someone he could trust at the top of the empire. He could have looked for the most able person he could find, but he turned to Basilius. Basilius knew horses and had no experience of government.

Michael gave his friend wealth and raised him to high rank. He believed so much kindness would bind Basilius to him forever, but Basilius kept wanting more. Basilius persuaded Michael that Michael's uncle was ambitious and might plot against him, and he got Michael to agree to have the uncle killed. When Michael later asked for money back, Basilius refused, and Michael finally saw how much power his friend now held. After a night of heavy drinking, soldiers killed Michael while Basilius watched, and Basilius took the throne. Michael picked his friend over the skill the job needed, and his warm feelings hid the danger until it was too late.

Now look at the opposite move, from China. A general had just become the first emperor of the Sung dynasty, in an age when generals kept seizing the throne. The emperor invited the army's most powerful commanders to a banquet and said plainly that any of them might want the throne. Then the emperor offered them titles and fine estates if they would step down, and they agreed. An old enemy got very different treatment. A defeated rival ruler was spared and brought to court. Offered a cup of wine, the rival feared it was poison. The emperor drank it instead, and the rival stayed loyal from then on. Old friends kept their comfort but lost their power, while an old enemy had every reason to prove loyal.

You don't have to go as far as the law does. You can stay close to your friends and simply stop handing them jobs they can't do. When a job really matters, start by writing down what it takes, then look for the person who can do it. That person might be a stranger, or even an old rival who once beat you. The same goes for home, where a cousin who offers to rewire your kitchen may be kind but not trained. Saying no to a friend's offer stings for a day, but a ruined job can sour a friendship for years.

Back at the restaurant, Noor writes down what the job takes: clean records, tax rules, and a steady eye on the cash. Callum has none of that training, and she can see it once it's on paper. She thanks him warmly and explains the choice face to face. The bookkeeper's work can be checked and corrected, which would feel rude with a friend. If a mistake happens, she can say so without risking anything but a job.

The law has one exception of its own. A friend can be more useful than an enemy for dirty work, or as someone to take the blame when a plan fails. But once you make a friend take the blame, you have lost that friend for good. Few of us would ever want that trade, and you never have to make it. So Noor hires the bookkeeper and keeps Callum for Sunday dinners. The skilled stranger is the safer pick, because liking someone can stop you checking what they can do. Let the job pick the person, and let your friends stay friends.

examples.title: The night shift needs a leader
examples.scenario: Kwame manages a busy warehouse and must name a night shift supervisor before the holiday rush. Dario, his closest friend at work, asks for the job over lunch, though he has never led a team. Sofia, a quiet coworker Kwame barely knows, ran shifts at a bigger warehouse for years. The form is due at five, and Kwame picks up the pen to fill in a name.
examples.whatToDo: Name Sofia, because the job needs someone who has run shifts. Tell Dario why in person, and keep your lunches going.
examples.whyItMatters: The rush gets a proven leader, and Kwame and Dario stay friends instead of becoming a boss and a resentful worker.

examples.title: Your debate final needs a partner
examples.scenario: Amara has to pick one partner for the debate final, which decides her place on the school team. Joon, her best friend, is waving from across the room, but he hates speaking in public. Tessa, the classmate who beat her in last month's debate, is still free. The teacher looks up from the list and asks Amara to call out a name.
examples.whatToDo: Pick Tessa, because the final needs a strong speaker, and tell Joon you'll still meet after class as usual.
examples.whyItMatters: A rival who has beaten you has real skill and something to prove, and your friendship with Joon stays safe.

examples.title: A free wedding photographer
examples.scenario: Hana is getting married in the spring and needs a photographer. Luca, her oldest friend, just bought a nice camera and offers to do it for free. A local photographer with years of wedding work would cost real money. Luca sends a happy text saying the date is already in the calendar, and she starts to type a reply.
examples.whatToDo: Thank Luca warmly, book the trained photographer, and ask him to come as a guest and enjoy the day.
examples.whyItMatters: A wedding can't be shot twice, and Luca gets to be Hana's friend that day, not a stressed worker.

questions.prompt: Your small theater group needs someone to handle ticket money for its biggest show. Your close friend offers, but they often lose receipts. A member you barely know does accounts for a living. What do you do?
choices: Give it to your friend, since you know you can rely on them.
Give it to the member who does accounts, and thank your friend.
Split the job between them, so nobody's feelings get hurt at all.
questions.explanation: The job needs skill, so the person who does accounts should get it. Trusting your friend mistakes warmth for ability. Splitting the job only avoids the choice and still puts money in weak hands.

questions.prompt: A gym owner makes a best friend the new manager, though the friend has never run anything. Soon members leave, and the owner can't bring it up. What thinking caused the trouble?
choices: Thinking a close friend would be a safe pick, skills or no skills.
Thinking gym members would stay no matter who ran the place each day.
Thinking the friend needed a higher wage to keep working hard for them.
questions.explanation: The owner trusted the friendship and never checked the skill, so warm feelings hid the gap. Members leaving is the result, not the cause, and pay had nothing to do with it.

questions.prompt: A band needs a sound engineer for its first album. The singer skips a longtime pal and hires a stranger who has mixed many records. What most likely happens next?
choices: The album suffers, because a stranger won't care the way a pal would.
The pal takes over anyway, because friends always find a way back in.
The album sounds good, and the singer and pal stay easy together.
questions.explanation: Picking on skill gets the work done well, and the friendship stays out of it. Expecting a stranger not to care assumes that only friends can be relied on.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "I'm making my buddy my business partner. I've known them forever, so I know they won't let me down." What is your best reply?
choices: Knowing someone isn't knowing their skills, so check what the job takes.
Good call, since nobody is safer in business than someone you've long known.
Bad call, since old friends always betray you once they get some money.
questions.explanation: Friends can hide their faults, so check the skills first. Agreeing repeats the idea that a friend can't let you down. Saying friends always betray you goes too far, because the fix is judging the work.

questions.prompt: A food truck owner needed a cook. They passed over a friend and hired a cook who used to work for a rival truck. Sales rose, and the friendship lasted. Why did this work?
choices: The friend would surely have tried to take over the whole business.
The owner chose on skill, so the friendship never carried the job.
The new cook only worked hard because the pay was so much better.
questions.explanation: The job went to the person who could do it, so the friend stayed a friend. Assuming the friend would betray the owner goes past the facts, and nothing suggests pay drove the result.

questions.prompt: You need a lawyer to sort out a family house sale. Your golf buddy is a lawyer who handles only traffic cases, and they offer a friendly discount. What do you do?
choices: Hire your buddy, since a friend will look after you on this one.
Hire no one, and sort out the house sale yourself to keep the peace.
Hire a lawyer who does house sales, and keep golf as it is.
questions.explanation: The job needs house sale skill, which your buddy doesn't have. Taking the discount trusts friendship over ability. Doing it yourself avoids an awkward talk, but the job still lacks the right skill.

questions.prompt: A team leader lets a close friend take the public blame for a failed product. The leader keeps their job, but the friend never speaks to them again. What thinking caused the trouble?
choices: Thinking a friend could be sacrificed and still stay a friend.
Thinking the failed product was a small problem for the company.
Thinking the friend should have taken the blame much more quietly.
questions.explanation: Using a friend to take the blame costs you that friend for good. The size of the failure and how quietly the friend took it are side issues, because the sacrifice ended the friendship.

reviewCards.front: Your hiking club needs a treasurer, and your best friend says they'd love to do it, though they've never kept accounts.
reviewCards.back: List what the job takes, choose the member who can do it, and tell your friend why, so the money and the friendship both stay safe.

reviewCards.front: Your dental office needs a new office manager. Why look past the friend who asks first?
reviewCards.back: Because liking someone tells you nothing about their skill, and a friend may hide faults or agree with you to keep the peace.

reviewCards.front: When a friend asks for a job you can't be sure they can do, the first thing to check is ...
reviewCards.back: ... what the job takes, because a warm feeling can hide a gap in skill, and the work needs skill first.

reviewCards.front: A dog groomer hired a close pal as an assistant, and the pal kept missing bookings. The groomer said nothing for months, and the regulars drifted away.
reviewCards.back: They chose friendship over skill, and then the friendship made it hard to speak plainly. A skilled stranger could have been corrected after the first missed booking.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what does 'hire skill, not friendship' mean, and why does it work?
reviewCards.back: When a job really matters, pick the person who can do it and keep friends as friends, because warm feelings can hide weak skills.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Judge who should do an important job by the skill it takes, before liking or old ties choose for you.

ifThenPlans.plan: When a friend says, "I can do that for you, no problem" about a job that really matters, I ask what similar work they've done before I say yes.
When I catch myself typing a friend's name into a hiring form or group chat for a key role, I stop, write down the skills the job needs, and check the name against them.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before bed tonight, pick one job a friend now does for you. Ask whether you would hire them for it if they were a stranger, and write down your honest answer.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each time you sit down to plan your week, pick the most important task ahead. Write who will do it and the skill that earned them the job, not the friendship.

chapters.title: Keep Your Real Goal Quiet Until the Plan Moves
chapters.hook: The people most likely to block your plan are often the ones you just told about it. Say your goal out loud, and you hand them time to get in your way. So what should you keep quiet?
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think telling others exactly what they want earns respect and help. Actually, it works better to keep your real goal quiet until your plan is moving, because people can only block what they see coming.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Keep your real goal to yourself until your plan is moving, because people can block only what they see coming.
chapters.tryThisNow: Write down one plan you have today, like a job hunt or a big purchase, and list who does not need to know yet. Fewer people knowing means fewer people in your way.

memorableLines.text: Let them see the plan only after it is already moving.

breakdown.fastRead:

A young French marquis learned this the hard way. He asked the famous charmer Ninon de Lenclos how to win a countess. She told him to come at it sideways and keep the countess guessing, and soon the countess was curious. Then he blurted out his love, and her interest died. Bismarck did the opposite. Known as a fierce man, he wanted war with Austria, yet he gave a speech praising peace with Austria. Prussia's king trusted him and gave him a high post. Years later, Bismarck used that power to lead Prussia into that war. Nobody could block an aim they never saw.

Once you are known as a schemer, no cover works, so the rule says to play the honest rascal in the open. So Ines can learn the job quietly and apply when the post opens. Let your plan get moving before anyone knows your goal, because nobody can block what they never saw coming.

breakdown.fullRead:
Telling people your goal often hands them the tools to stop you. Ines works at a travel agency and wants the branch manager job that opens in the spring. At Friday's staff lunch, she plans to tell everyone. She hopes the openness will win friends and maybe a word of support from the boss. Instead, it will start a quiet race that she cannot see yet. By Monday, the race will already be running.

This hope feels right because we are taught that honest people get rewarded. Saying what you want seems brave, and hiding it seems sneaky. But a goal said out loud is a map for everyone else. A coworker who wants the same job starts lining up support before Ines has even applied. Another quietly tells the boss that she is not ready yet. People are not cruel for doing this. They simply get ready for what they can see coming, and a clear aim is easy to see.

Most people go through life as open books. They say what they feel, they show what they want, and they explain their plans to anyone who asks. That makes them easy to read and easy to block. The rule asks you to work the other way. People tend to take what you show them at face value, so they judge you by your manner and your words. A calm, friendly face draws little notice. So does a plan that seems to point somewhere else. While people watch the thing you seem to want, your real aim moves forward out of sight.

A young French marquis learned this the hard way. He wanted to win a countess, so he asked the famous charmer Ninon de Lenclos for advice. She told him not to chase the countess openly. He should come at it sideways, act a little cool, and keep the countess guessing about what he felt. He followed the plan, and at first it worked. The countess grew more and more curious about this young man she could not quite read.

Then the marquis could not hold back. One day he let it all spill out, blurting out his love and telling her plainly what he wanted. Once she knew his whole aim, there was nothing left to wonder about. Her interest died, and all his careful work came undone at once. Nothing about him had changed except that his goal was now in plain view. While she was guessing, she kept leaning in, but once she knew, she pulled away.

Otto von Bismarck did the opposite. Everyone in Prussia knew him as a fierce man who loved a fight, and he wanted war with Austria. So people expected him to cheer for that war. Yet he stood up and gave a speech praising peace with Austria. Prussia's king trusted him and gave him a high post. Years later, Bismarck used that power to lead Prussia into the very war he had wanted. Had he called for war early, he might never have gained the power to start it. The marquis showed his aim and lost, while Bismarck hid his and nobody stood in his way.

At full strength, the rule says never show anyone why you act. Lead people down the wrong path, and wrap them in so much smoke that they see your aim only when it is too late. For you, it is enough to keep quiet, not to lie or trick anyone. That alone covers a lot of daily life. You can look for a new job without telling your team. You can walk onto a car lot without saying your top price. At home, you can plan a big move without announcing it before the details are set.

So Ines can skip the big speech at Friday's lunch. She can learn more about the manager's work, take on a few bigger tasks, and do strong work with clients. When the post opens, she applies, and by then the case is already built. A rival has little time to line up support against a plan that is nearly done. Ines has not lied to anyone along the way. She has simply kept her goal private until it was ready to be seen.

Greene sets one clear boundary on this rule. If people already know you as someone who plays games, no cover will work, because they will suspect everything you do. Then the rule turns around and says to play the honest rascal in the open, since that face can still hide your plans. Greene offers no exception for loved ones, but with a partner or close friend, where trust is the whole point, it is wise to share more than you would at work. For most plans, though, the move is simple. Let your plan get moving before anyone knows your goal, because nobody can block what they never saw coming.

examples.title: The interview nobody needs to hear about
examples.scenario: Kenji is a vet tech at an animal clinic and has a second interview at a clinic across town on Thursday. Nothing is signed yet. In the break room, the practice manager asks why Kenji wants Thursday off. He likes the manager and hates hiding things. A full, honest answer is right on the tip of his tongue, and the manager is waiting.
examples.whatToDo: Say you have a personal errand that day, and keep the interview private until you have a signed offer in hand.
examples.whyItMatters: If the move falls through, Kenji keeps a good job and a manager who never started doubting his loyalty.

examples.title: The club vote you want to win
examples.scenario: Yusuf wants to be president of the college photography club, and the vote is in three weeks. He has ideas for a new darkroom schedule and a bigger spring show. At tonight's meeting, members are chatting about who might run. Someone turns to him and asks, "Are you going for it?" The whole table goes quiet, waiting for an answer.
examples.whatToDo: Say it's too early to know, then spend the next weeks quietly helping plan the spring show so members see your ideas work.
examples.whyItMatters: By the time anyone hears Yusuf is running, members have already watched his ideas succeed, so a rival has little to push against.

examples.title: The piano you would pay full price for
examples.scenario: Elif found a used upright piano online and is now standing in the seller's living room. She loves it and would pay the full asking price if needed. The seller smiles and asks, "So what were you hoping to spend?" Her partner, standing nearby, opens their mouth to answer for both of them, and Elif has a second to decide.
examples.whatToDo: Jump in kindly, ask what the seller would take for a quick sale today, and keep your top number to yourself.
examples.whyItMatters: Once the seller hears Elif's limit, that limit becomes the price, so staying quiet keeps room to pay less.

questions.prompt: You plan to leave your job at a grocery chain in six months to open your own bakery. Coworkers ask about your weekend baking class. What do you do?
choices: Tell them about the bakery plan, so they can cheer you on and spread the word.
Say you enjoy baking for fun, and keep the bakery plan quiet for now.
Tell them you hate baking and only took the class for a friend.
questions.explanation: Keeping the plan quiet until it is moving means nobody at work can act on it early. Sharing it all invites trouble before you are ready. Making up a lie is more than you need and can catch you out.

questions.prompt: A neighbor wants to buy the empty lot next door to plant a small orchard. They tell the whole street first. A developer hears and buys the lot within weeks. What was the mistake?
choices: They thought telling everyone would bring help, but it warned a rival buyer.
They waited too long to tell the street, so support came too slowly.
They should have kept the plan secret from the developer only.
questions.explanation: The open plan gave a rival time to move first. Telling sooner would only have warned the developer sooner. And on a busy street, you can't pick who hears your news.

questions.prompt: A swim coach wants to move practice to a better pool. The coach quietly books trial lanes and gathers parent sign-ups before telling the other coach, who likes the old pool. What most likely happens?
choices: The other coach is thankful, because quiet plans always feel friendly.
The other coach blocks the move, since secret plans always get found out.
The move is mostly set before the other coach can push back.
questions.explanation: By the time the other coach hears, the lanes and sign-ups are in place, so little is left to block. Plans tend to fail when they are seen early, not when they are already moving.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "I'm going to tell my landlord I'd pay anything to keep this apartment. Being honest will make them like me." What is your best reply?
choices: Good idea, since landlords reward tenants who are open and direct.
Ask the new rent first, and keep your limit to yourself.
Say you're moving out anyway, so they drop the price right away.
questions.explanation: Once the landlord hears you would pay anything, that becomes the rent. Asking first keeps your limit private. Bluffing that you are leaving is a lie that could cost you the apartment.

questions.prompt: A pharmacy clerk wants to run a weekend candle stall. They test recipes at home and tell their boss only once the stall is booked and selling. The boss can't talk them out of it. Why did this work?
choices: The stall was already running, so nothing was left to stop.
The boss respected the clerk's honesty in telling them the plan.
The secret made the boss curious, so they wanted to support it.
questions.explanation: People can block only what they see coming, and by the time the boss heard, the plan was set. The honesty came late, so it was not the reason. Curiosity had nothing to do with it.

questions.prompt: You want to ask your cousin for a job at their catering business, but your aunt loves to gossip and works there too. At a family barbecue, the aunt asks what you're up to. What do you do?
choices: Tell her about the job idea, since family will want to help you.
Say you are about to move abroad, so she stops asking questions.
Mention your current work, and save the job talk for your cousin.
questions.explanation: Talking to your cousin directly keeps your aim from spreading before you ask. Telling the aunt sends it around the family first. A fake move abroad is a lie you would have to undo.

questions.prompt: A coworker is known all over the office for playing games and working angles. They start keeping their next project secret and acting extra mysterious. People push back harder than ever. What went wrong?
choices: They should have told everyone everything, since honesty always earns help.
Once known as a schemer, secrecy only made people more suspicious.
They should have hidden it better with a cleverer cover story.
questions.explanation: Hiding works only while people trust you. A known schemer's secrets look like more games, so being open about who you are works better. A cleverer cover story fails for the same reason.

reviewCards.front: You're buying a used boat at a marina, and the seller asks the most you can spend.
reviewCards.back: Ask for their best price first and keep your limit to yourself, because the number you say out loud quickly becomes the price.

reviewCards.front: You've applied to grad school but haven't been accepted yet. Why might it help to keep it quiet at work for now?
reviewCards.back: Because people can only react to what they know, so you keep your job steady and avoid doubts until the plan is set.

reviewCards.front: When you're planning a big change, the best time to tell people your real goal is ...
reviewCards.back: ... after your plan is already moving, because by then there is little left for anyone to block.

reviewCards.front: A tenant told the building owner they planned to start a petition for repairs. A week later, the owner had sent every tenant a letter calling the repairs unneeded.
reviewCards.back: The warning let the owner get ready first. Gathering signatures quietly, then sharing the petition, would have left the owner no time to push back.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what does 'hide the aim' mean, and why does it work?
reviewCards.back: Keep what you're really after private until your plan is moving, because people can't block what they don't see coming.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Keep your real goal private until your plan is already moving, so nobody has time to block it.

ifThenPlans.plan: When a coworker leans over at the coffee machine and asks, "So what are your plans this year?", I share one small, true thing I'm working on and keep my bigger goal to myself.
When a salesperson on the phone asks, "What's your budget?", I ask what their best price is first and keep my top number off the table.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before bed tonight, pick one goal you have been talking about too freely. Choose the next quiet step you can take on it this week, and take it without telling anyone.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each Sunday evening, look at your plans for the week. For each one, ask who truly needs to know now, and wait to tell anyone else until that step is done.

chapters.title: Why Saying Less Protects You
chapters.hook: Your manager has given you ten minutes to make the case for a raise, and you have twelve reasons down. More reasons should make a stronger case. So why might reason number twelve be the one that sinks you?
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think that explaining yourself fully, and saying everything you feel, will win people over. Actually, a short point said once and left alone lands harder, because every extra sentence is another chance to say something you cannot take back.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Make your point in a few words, then stop, because every extra sentence is another chance to hurt yourself.
chapters.tryThisNow: Cut your next request email or text today down to three sentences before you send it. Every line you remove is one less line that can be read the wrong way.

memorableLines.text: Every sentence after your point is a sentence that can turn on you.

breakdown.fastRead:
Ten minutes with the print shop manager is all Idris gets to ask for a raise, and he has a page of reasons ready. His plan is to cover everything, from the extra shifts to how unfair it is that a slower coworker earns the same. Saying it all feels safe, because we are taught that the whole story wins people over. But every extra point is one more thing the manager can doubt or hold against him.

A Roman war hero named Coriolanus learned this the hard way. Running for a top office in Rome, he showed the crowd his battle scars. The people were moved and ready to vote for him. On election day he came with powerful nobles, bragged about himself, and talked down to the voters, so they turned against him. He lost the vote. Later he gave an angry speech saying the common people should not get grain, and the outrage drove him out of the city for good. His scars won the crowd, and his own words lost it.

The rule of power goes further. Talk a lot and you seem common and less in control, so say little and let people guess. You do not need to act mysterious, but you can stop before you hurt yourself. Just know that too much silence can make a boss suspicious. So Idris can name the extra shifts, ask for the raise, and stop. Make your point in a few words, and then let it stand.
breakdown.deepRead:
Ten minutes with the print shop manager is all Idris gets to ask for a raise, and he has a page of reasons ready. His plan is to cover everything. There are the extra shifts, the rush orders he handled alone, and the customers who now ask for him by name. Then there is the slower coworker who earns the same pay, which feels deeply unfair. He is sure that the full list will win the case. But somewhere around the seventh reason, the manager will stop listening and start judging.

Saying it all feels right because it is how most of us learned to argue. In school, an essay with more reasons often got the better grade. But a talk about money with a boss is not a school essay. Each extra point gives the listener one more thing to doubt, and a weak point drags the strong ones down. The line about the coworker is the worst, because it makes Idris sound petty instead of valuable. Once it is said, it cannot be taken back.

A Roman war hero named Coriolanus learned this the hard way. He had won great battles, and the people of Rome loved him for it. When he ran for a top office, he showed the crowd his battle scars. The people were moved and ready to vote for him. But on election day he arrived with a group of powerful nobles. He bragged about himself and talked down to the voters, so they turned on him and he lost. Later he gave an angry speech against the common people and argued that they should not get grain. The outrage was so great that he was driven out of the city for good. His scars had won the crowd, and his own words threw it away.

The rule of power behind this is blunt. The more you talk, the more common and less in control you seem. Say less, keep your words vague and open-ended, and even a banal remark will sound original. Every extra word also raises the chance of saying something foolish. You do not need to act mysterious, but you can stop before you hurt yourself. Silence has limits, because a boss who hears too little may wonder what you are hiding. So Idris can name the extra shifts and the loyal customers, ask for the raise, and stop. Make your point in a few words, and then let it stand.
breakdown.fullRead:
Ten minutes with the print shop manager is all Idris gets to ask for a raise, and he has a page of reasons ready. His plan is to cover everything. There are the extra shifts, the rush orders he handled alone, and the customers who now ask for him by name. Then there is the slower coworker who earns the same pay, which feels deeply unfair. He is sure that the full list will win the case. But somewhere around the seventh reason, the manager will stop listening and start judging. The manager may never say so, and Idris may walk out thinking it went well.

Saying it all feels right because it is how most of us learned to argue. In school, an essay with more reasons often got the better grade. With friends, talking through your feelings in full is how you get understood. But a talk about money with a boss is not a chat with a friend. Each extra point gives the listener one more thing to doubt, and a weak point drags the strong ones down. The line about the coworker is the worst, because it makes Idris sound petty instead of valuable. Once it is said, it cannot be taken back.

The rule of power behind this is blunt. The more you talk, the more common and less in control you seem. People with real power impress others, and even unsettle them, by holding back. Say less, stay vague and open-ended, and even a banal remark will sound original, because listeners fill the gaps with their own guesses. Talk too much and you show your hand, your worries, and your weak spots. Every extra word also raises the chance of saying something foolish. Once others have heard a foolish sentence, you can never pull it back.

A Roman war hero named Coriolanus learned this the hard way. He had won great battles for Rome, and the people loved him for his courage. In time he decided to run for a top office in the city. When he went out to meet the crowd, he did something simple. He showed the people his battle scars. The scars told his story for him. The people were moved, and they were ready to vote for him.

Then came election day. Coriolanus arrived with a group of powerful nobles at his side. Instead of letting his record speak, he started talking. He bragged about his own deeds and talked down to the very voters he needed. The same people who had been moved by his scars now saw a proud man who looked down on them. They turned against him, and he lost. Nothing about his courage had changed between those two moments. The only new thing was how much he said.

Then he made things worse. Later he gave an angry speech against the common people and argued that they should not get grain. The public outrage was so great that he was driven out of Rome for good. A hero who had needed only his scars to win the crowd lost his place in the city through a couple of speeches. His scars had won people over, and his own words threw it all away.

None of this means you should go quiet or act like a riddle. The harsh version of the rule asks you to seem mysterious and a little frightening. You can keep the useful part, which is simply stopping before you hurt yourself. At work, that means making your point, giving one reason, and then letting the other person speak. At home, it means saying the one thing that matters in a hard talk, without the old complaints that come rushing in behind it. When a silence follows your point, let it sit, because rushing to fill it often adds the sentence you regret. The point you make in a few words is the point people remember.

So Idris can walk into the manager's office with a shorter page. He can name the extra shifts and the customers who ask for him by name, then ask for the raise. The complaint about the coworker stays out, because it adds nothing and could cost a lot. When the manager goes quiet to think, Idris can wait instead of adding reason number eight. His case is smaller, but there is nothing weak in it for the manager to grab.

Saying less has its own limits. Too much silence can make people suspicious, especially the people above you. A boss who gets only short, cold answers may start to wonder what you are hiding. Sometimes talking a lot is the better cover. Like a court jester, a person who chatters can seem harmless, and the chatter can hide a trick underneath. Most days, though, the move is simple. Make your point in a few words, and then let it stand.

examples.title: The late project at your review
examples.scenario: Marisol runs installs at a solar panel company, and a big rooftop job finished two weeks late. In the review meeting, the operations director asks one question: what happened? Marisol has a long answer ready about the late parts, the rainy weeks, and the crew member who kept calling in sick. She takes a breath and is about to start at the beginning.
examples.whatToDo: Give the main cause and the fix in two sentences, such as late parts and a new supplier, then stop and wait for questions.
examples.whyItMatters: A long list sounds like excuses, and blaming a sick coworker could make her look like the problem.

examples.title: The extension email to your professor
examples.scenario: Ingrid missed a week of a college statistics course with the flu and needs more time on a big paper. Her email draft is already four paragraphs long. It covers her fever, a roommate who kept the lights on, and a line saying the deadline was too tight anyway. Her cursor is hovering over the send button.
examples.whatToDo: Cut it to three lines: you were sick, you would like one more week, and thank you. Delete the rest before sending.
examples.whyItMatters: The line about the tight deadline insults the professor, so one extra sentence could turn an easy yes into a no.

examples.title: The apology that keeps growing
examples.scenario: Rafael forgot to pick up a friend from the train station late at night, and the friend waited over an hour in the cold. He calls to apologize. His words are ready: sorry, then his busy week, his phone on silent, and a reminder that the friend was late last month too. The friend picks up and says hello.
examples.whatToDo: Say you are sorry, say it will not happen again, and offer to make it up. Then stop and let your friend talk.
examples.whyItMatters: Excuses shrink the apology, and the jab about last month could turn a short hurt into a real fight.

questions.prompt: Your landlord agrees to fix a drafty window but asks why it has to be this week. You have a long list of reasons ready. What do you do?
choices: Walk through every reason, so the landlord sees how serious it is.
Give the one main reason, like the cold getting in, then stop.
Say nothing about why, so you seem calm and in control.
questions.explanation: One clear reason answers the question, and stopping keeps you from adding something that weakens it. Listing every reason feels thorough but gives the landlord more to doubt. Saying nothing dodges a fair question.

questions.prompt: A job candidate is asked why they left their last job. They explain at length and end by calling their old boss lazy. They don't get the offer. What belief led them wrong?
choices: Believing they should have refused to answer such a personal question.
Believing a short answer was safest, so they kept it brief.
Believing a full, honest explanation would win the interviewer over.
questions.explanation: They thought saying everything would earn trust. Each extra sentence gave them another chance to slip, and the jab at the old boss did the damage. They did not keep it brief, and refusing to answer would have hurt them too.

questions.prompt: A parent asks a youth soccer coach to give their child more playing time. They make one clear point about the child's progress, then stop. What most likely happens next?
choices: The coach takes it seriously, since there's nothing weak to argue with.
The coach brushes it off, since such a short request sounds unimportant.
The coach agrees on the spot, since short requests always get a yes.
questions.explanation: One clear point gives the coach nothing weak to push back on, so it gets weighed fairly. More words would not have made it stronger. Being brief helps, but it guarantees nothing.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "My neighbor's tree keeps dropping branches on my car. I'm writing them a long letter about everything that's bugged me since they moved in." What is your best reply?
choices: Good idea, the more they hear, the better they'll understand you.
Skip the letter and just wait, since saying anything could backfire.
Ask about the branches in a few lines, and leave the rest out.
questions.explanation: A short note about the branches makes the one point that matters. Old complaints give the neighbor reasons to get defensive. Waiting in silence just leaves the branches landing on the car.

questions.prompt: A delivery driver wants a different route and texts the dispatcher two clear sentences. The change is approved within the hour. Why did this work?
choices: The short text gave the dispatcher nothing extra to doubt or argue with.
The text explained all the driver's reasons, so the dispatcher understood.
Short texts always get approved, so the length alone won the day.
questions.explanation: A short ask leaves nothing weak to pick at, so it is easy to approve. It worked because the driver stopped early, not because every reason was spelled out. Length alone guarantees nothing.

questions.prompt: In a team meeting, you propose moving the weekly report to Mondays. Nobody responds right away, and the silence feels awkward. What do you do?
choices: Keep explaining your idea from new angles until someone agrees.
Let the quiet sit, and wait for someone else to respond.
Take the idea back, since the quiet means people dislike it.
questions.explanation: Your point is made, so filling the silence only adds chances to weaken it. Explaining it again makes you sound unsure. Pulling the idea back reads too much into a short pause.

questions.prompt: A new hire gives only one-word answers in every meeting with the boss, hoping to seem strong. Soon the boss asks others if the new hire is unhappy or hiding something. What was the mistake?
choices: Going so quiet that the boss wondered what was being hidden.
Not telling the boss every thought and feeling about the new job.
Being too short with coworkers, who then complained to the boss.
questions.explanation: Saying less has limits, and too much silence makes the people above you suspicious. The fix is clear, short answers, not every feeling poured out. Coworkers were not the issue here.

reviewCards.front: Your teenager asks why they can't go to a late concert on a school night, and you feel a long lecture coming on.
reviewCards.back: Give the one real reason, like the early test, and stop there, because every extra point gives them something new to argue with.

reviewCards.front: You're asking a board to approve your budget. Why would cutting your case from ten reasons to two make it stronger?
reviewCards.back: Because each weak reason gives the board something to doubt and drags the strong ones down. Two solid reasons leave nothing to pick at.

reviewCards.front: When you've made your point and the room goes quiet, the best thing to say next is ...
reviewCards.back: ... nothing for a moment, because rushing to fill the silence only adds chances to weaken what you just said.

reviewCards.front: A tenant asked the building manager for a parking spot, then kept talking and mentioned sometimes parking in the fire lane. The request was denied.
reviewCards.back: They kept going after the point was made, and one extra sentence handed the manager a reason to say no.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what does 'say it, then stop' mean, and why does it work?
reviewCards.back: Make your point in a few words and end there, because every sentence you add is another chance to hurt yourself.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Make your point in a few clear words, then stop talking and let it stand.

ifThenPlans.plan: When my manager leans back at our one-on-one and says, "Walk me through what happened", I give the main cause and my fix in two sentences, and wait for their next question.
When a text I'm writing to my partner grows past the top of my phone screen, I delete everything but the one thing I need them to know, and send that.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In your next meeting or phone call today, make one point in a single sentence. Then count to five in your head before saying anything else, and notice how the other person responds.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each Friday, reread three messages you sent that week. Find one sentence in each that you could have left out, and ask whether it made the message weaker.

chapters.title: Be Known for One Thing, and Let Your Name Go First
chapters.hook: You and a coworker hand in work of the same quality. Yours gets questioned line by line, and theirs gets a quick nod. Nobody checked which was better. So what were people reacting to before they even looked?
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think good work speaks for itself, so how others see you hardly matters. Actually, people judge your work through your name before they look at it, because a clear reputation tells them what to expect.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Pick one clear quality to be known for, so people react to your name before you act.
chapters.tryThisNow: Write the one quality you want to be known for, like steady or fair, on a sticky note by your screen today. Then act on it once before evening, because a name grows from small repeats.

memorableLines.text: Choose one thing to be known for, and let your name arrive first.

breakdown.fastRead:
Why does Esther's building plan pass review in five minutes, while Kofi's plan, just as good, gets picked apart for an hour? Both work at the same architecture firm. Kofi believes good work speaks for itself, because that is how tests were marked at school. But people rarely look at work fresh, so they judge it through the name on top.

In ancient China, the general Chuko Liang was resting in a small town with only a few soldiers. Then a huge army under Sima Yi marched toward it. Fighting was hopeless, and running was too. So Chuko Liang threw open the city gates, sat on the wall, and calmly played music. Sima Yi knew Chuko Liang's name for clever tricks, feared a trap, and pulled back. Years spent building one sharp reputation did the fighting, because the enemy was beaten by what he expected.

At its harshest, the law says to make your name too solid to attack. It also says to sink rivals by poking holes in their names, then let gossip finish them. For you, the fair move is to guard only your own name. And there is never a time to stop caring, because a name you neglect gets written by others. Esther is known for one thing, catching mistakes, so the partners relax before they read. Kofi can build a name like that too. Pick one clear quality and show it again and again, so people react to your name before you act.
